paragraphs.heading: What a critical point is
paragraphs.text: In thermodynamics, a critical point is where a phase equilibrium curve comes to an end. The liquid–vapor critical point is one example: the end of the pressure–temperature curve that marks the conditions where a liquid and its vapor can exist side by side. Its location is given by two numbers: T_c, the critical temperature, and p_c, the critical pressure; and at that spot the boundaries between phases disappear.

paragraphs.heading: On a phase diagram
paragraphs.text: On a pressure–temperature diagram of a pure substance, solid, liquid and vapor are divided by phase boundaries, the pressure and temperature combinations where two phases can coexist. At the triple point all three can coexist. The liquid–vapor boundary, however, does not run on forever: it stops at the critical temperature T_c and critical pressure p_c.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond the critical point
paragraphs.text: At higher temperatures the gas becomes supercritical, and pressure by itself cannot turn it into a liquid. This state, called a supercritical fluid, is continuously connected to both liquid and gas, so it can become either without a phase transition. Even above the critical temperature, though, enough pressure might still squeeze the matter into a solid. And the common textbook view that liquid and vapor become completely indistinguishable past this point has been challenged by Fisher and Widom.

paragraphs.heading: Water near its critical point
paragraphs.text: Water's critical point lies at 647.096 K (373.946 °C) and 22.064 megapascals. Approaching it, liquid and vapor change sharply and grow ever more alike. Ordinary liquid water is barely compressible, expands little with heat, has a high dielectric constant and dissolves electrolytes very well. Near the critical point each of these reverses: water becomes compressible and expandable, a poor dielectric and a bad solvent for electrolytes, and it mixes more easily with nonpolar gases and organic molecules.

paragraphs.heading: How it was found
paragraphs.text: No critical point was found earlier than the liquid–vapor one, and it remains the most studied and best known. Charles Cagniard de la Tour discovered that critical points exist in 1822; Dmitri Mendeleev named the idea in 1860, and Thomas Andrews in 1869. Cagniard found that carbon dioxide, CO₂, would turn liquid at 31 °C under 73 atm of pressure, but not at a slightly higher temperature, even at pressures as high as 3000 atm.

paragraphs.heading: Other kinds of critical point
paragraphs.text: Critical points appear in other settings too, such as the liquid–liquid critical points of mixtures and the Curie temperature, where a ferromagnet turns paramagnet with no outside magnetic field. In a solution, a liquid–liquid critical point sits at the edge of the two-phase region of the phase diagram. There, a tiny change in temperature or pressure splits the mixture into two distinct liquid phases. The upper critical solution temperature is the hottest point at which cooling causes this separation, and the lower one is the coldest point at which heating does.
